faqs.a: Yes. The bearing is computed with the standard great-circle formula on a spherical Earth, the same math used by navigation software. For the few thousand kilometres most users are from Makkah, the spherical model is accurate to well under a degree — far more precise than a phone compass can display.

The compass needle points along the computed bearing measured clockwise from true north. To face the Qibla, hold your phone flat, let its compass settle, and rotate your body until the needle points straight up (toward the N mark rotated by your bearing). In practice, align yourself with the needle direction on the dial.
faqs.q: How do I use the compass dial?

For most purposes, no. Rhumb-line (constant compass heading) and great-circle (shortest path) bearings to Makkah differ by a few degrees at most, and Islamic scholarship overwhelmingly uses the great-circle bearing. This tool uses the great-circle bearing.
faqs.q: Should I follow a great-circle or rhumb-line bearing?

faqs.a: Near the antipode of Makkah (a point in the South Pacific near French Polynesia), every direction is almost equally toward Makkah and the bearing becomes unstable. If you are within a few hundred kilometres of the antipode, any direction is approximately correct.
faqs.q: What if I am on the opposite side of the Earth from Makkah?

faqs.a: The tool rounds to the nearest of the 16 compass points (N, NNE, NE, and so on) for a quick reading, but the exact bearing in degrees is always shown — use the degree value when precision matters.
faqs.q: Why does it show both degrees and a compass point?

qibla-direction-finder.formula:
Great-circle initial bearing to the Kaaba (21.4225°N, 39.8262°E):
θ = atan2( sin(Δλ), cos(φ1)·tan(φ2) − sin(φ1)·cos(Δλ) )
bearing = (θ in degrees + 360) mod 360
φ1, λ1 = your latitude/longitude; φ2 = 21.4225°, Δλ = 39.8262° − λ1.
